t: Maximum of Absolute Value Expression — Sign Enumeration Trick
o: We need the maximum over all pairs (i, j) of |arr1[i]-arr1[j]| + |arr2[i]-arr2[j]| + |i-j|. Brute force checks all O(n^2) pairs, which is too slow for n = 40000. The key observation is that each absolute value can be expanded by choosing a sign: |x| = max(x, -x). For a fixed choice of signs s1, s2 ∈ {+1, -1}, the expression becomes one of four linear forms: (s1·arr1[i] + s2·arr2[i] + i) − (s1·arr1[j] + s2·arr2[j] + j). Since the true maximum must equal one of these sign combinations when we take the max over both orders of i and j, it suffices to compute, for each of the four sign patterns, the maximum minus minimum of the transformed value f(k) = ±arr1[k] ± arr2[k] + k. **Example 1:** with arr1=[1,2,3,4], arr2=[-1,4,5,6], taking signs (+,+): values are 0,6,8,10 → max−min = 10; trying (+,−): 2,-2,-2,-2 → 4; (−,+): 0,2,4,6 → 6; (−,−): 2,-6,-8,-10 → 12... but checking pair (3,0): |4-1|+|6-(-1)|+|3-0| = 3+7+3 = 13, which corresponds to signs (+,+) with reversed order — our max−min over (+,+) is actually 13? Recomputing: (+,+) gives 1-1+0=0, 2+4+1=7, 3+5+2=10, 4+6+3=13 → 13−0=13. ✓ **Example 2:** the answer 20 arises similarly from some sign pattern's max−min. Constraints (n up to 40000, values up to 10^6) mean an O(n) or O(n log n) solution is required.
k: |a| + |b| + |c| where c = i-j ≥ 0 after ordering can be written as max over 4 sign choices of (±a ± b + c).
For each fixed sign pattern, the answer is simply max(f) − min(f) over all indices, computable in one pass.
This reduces an O(n^2) pairwise problem to four O(n) linear scans.

a.i: Directly evaluate the expression for every ordered pair (i, j) and track the maximum. This is the most intuitive solution and matches the problem statement literally, but at n = 40000 it performs ~1.6 billion operations, which will time out. It serves as a correctness baseline for testing the optimal approach.

a.t: O(n^2) — nested loops over all pairs.

a.i: Order each pair so that i ≥ j, making |i-j| = i-j. Then |arr1[i]-arr1[j]| + |arr2[i]-arr2[j]| equals the maximum over the four sign choices s1, s2 ∈ {+1,-1} of (s1·arr1[i] + s2·arr2[i]) − (s1·arr1[j] + s2·arr2[j]). So the overall answer is max over the 4 patterns of [max_k(±arr1[k] ± arr2[k] + k) − min_k(±arr1[k] ± arr2[k] + k)]. Each pattern is evaluated in a single pass, giving O(n) total.
s: Compute f(k) = p*arr1[k] + q*arr2[k] + k for all k, tracking mx = max f and mn = min f in one pass.
a.t: O(n) — four linear passes over the arrays.
a.sp: O(1) — only running max/min per sign pattern.

w: In an interview, briefly mention brute force to show you understand the problem, then derive the sign-enumeration trick — it generalizes to any sum of absolute differences plus a known-sign term. Common pitfalls: forgetting that |i-j| already has a fixed sign once you assume i ≥ j (so only 4 patterns, not 8); integer overflow in C++/Java if using smaller types (values up to ~3×10^6 fit easily in int here, but be careful in variants); and handling n = 2 correctly (the loops handle it naturally). Edge cases: all-equal arrays give 0 contribution from arr terms, so the answer is n-1. Follow-ups: extend to three arrays (now 8 sign patterns), or to maximizing a weighted sum of absolute differences.
